newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Devaluation speculation sweeps Dhaka forex market.
newsitem.headline: Devaluation speculation sweeps Dhaka forex market.

text.p: Speculation of a devaluation in Bangladesh's currency swept the local market on Wednesday following a steep devaluation in the Pakistani rupee.
Analysts said the Bangladesh could slide by more than five percent against the U.S. dollar by year-end.
On Tuesday, Pakistan's central bank devalued the rupee 7.86 percent against the dollar in a move designed to encourage foreign remittances and boost foreign currency deposits.

Some analysts said Bangladesh could soon follow Pakistan's lead because the taka and the rupee are both pegged to the same currency basket, but opinion is divided on the ultimate effect of the rupee's devaluation on the local currency.
"Pakistan is not a major trading partner nor a competitor (of Bangladesh)," said Wahiduddin Mahmud, an economist and former economic adviser to the government.
But he added: "Bangladesh may go for devaluation of its currency because of falling reserves and a high balance of payment deficit."
But some foreign exchange dealers eyed the potential impact of the Pakistani currency devaluation on the local market.

"Given the economic fundamental issues of a higher current account deficit a year ago, lower foreign exchange reserves and inflationary pressure, probably the taka should come down," said Gill James, an economist with Standard Chartered Bank.
"Because of the inflation differential between Bangladesh and the United States, the taka should be at 45 against the dollar by the end of the year," she told Reuters.
The taka is currently trading at around 42.35/55 to the dollar.
James said the Indian and Pakistani currencies had fallen against the dollar "quite significantly."
The dealers forecast the taka would weaken to 52 against dollar by the end of 1997.
However, Mahmud doubted the taka would lose as much ground as the Pakistani rupee and said the central bank may opt instead to adjust the taka downwards in phases.
"We are committed to flexible foreign exchange rates," said Mahmud, adding that "we are trying to mimic the free market economy."
Dealers said reserves were falling because of higher imports, a fall in export earnings and outflow of funds due to offloading of shares by foreign firms.

Bangladesh's foreign exchange reserves fell to $1.97 billion at the end of September from $2.06 billion in August and $2.68 billion in September 1995. The reserves have come down from their peak at $3.4 billion in April last year, according to central bank figures.
The country's current account deficit widened to an estimated $1.6 billion in fiscal 1995/96 (July-June) from $1.03 billion in the previous year.
The central Bangladesh Bank readjusted the taka against the dollar last on September 23 at 42.35/55, from 42.20/40.
Dealers said the taka had been adjusted downwards by only 4.18 percent since January 1996, compared to 17.25 percent for the Pakistani rupee.
